In each of the assessments , the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs . 1 , 50 , 000 estimated as the accrued interest on the amount owed investments . The assessee claimed that it had not been able to determine the surplus profits of the assessee ' s money lending investments but had paid only an amount equal to the accrued interests on the amounts lent investments . On appeal by the Revenue , the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Income Tax Officer . Hence this reference under section 27 ( 1 ) of the Wealth tax Act , 1957 , which was heard along with the appeals by the revenue . The Tribunal held that the provisions of section 3 of the Gift Tax Act were applicable to the case of the assessees and accordingly they were deleted from the list of assets maintained on cash basis . The High Court also held that since the accounts of the company were maintained on Cash basis interest due on accrual basis would be payable at the rate prescribed under the Income tax Act . The question whether the provisions contained in section 3 are applicable to cases where the account is maintained on a particular valuation date does not arise . The respondent was a Time Keeper in Be as Sut le j Link Project , Sundernagar . He was incharge of preparing pay bills and other bills of the work charg ed employees of the project . It was alleged that he ma de a sum of Rs . 238 90 as pay m ent card in the name of Ashok Kumar T . No . 59 T with the sign a ture of the issuing officer was prepared by the r espondent though it was not his duty to prepare the chair s for withdrawal of salary in t he name of one Shri Ashok Kumar . The said fictitious identity card was used by him for withdrawing the pay of the said Shri Ashok Kr . T . The respondent made an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal under Rule 5 ( 1 ) of the Central Civil Services ( Classification Control and Appeal ) Rules , 1965 for setting aside the order of penalty imposed on him . The Tribunal held that the respondent had committed misconduct and therefore , the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon him was harsh and disproportionate . In appeal , the Tribunal held against the respondent holding that the penalty was too low and that the Tribunal was justified in interfering with the punishment awarded to him . On appeal , this Court , HELD : 1 . 1 The respondent failed into the category of a workman and the Tribunal could exercise the powers of an industrial court for giving appropriate relief to the employee . [ 10 E F ] 2 . 1 There is no provision in the Act or any rule which provides for the appellate authority to review its own orders . [ 11 G H ; 12 A B ] 3 . 1 Section 4 of the Act empowers the Central Government to make rules regulating the conditions of service of persons appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any State . The proviso to sub section ( 1 ), however , says that the rules shall be subject to the ad mis sion that may be made by rules made under this Act . [ 12 D F ] 3 .( i ) The power conferred by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution is wide enough to include within its ambit all executive actions taken by the State in relation to the administration of justice . The power of judicial review is limited only to see whether the decision making process has been properly conducted or not . [ 13 G H ] 3 ( ii ) The High Court was right in interfering in the matter of imposition of lesser penalty than what was prescribed by the statute . [ 14 G H ].

The appellants , who were the legal representatives of one of the deceased plaintiff in a suit filed by him against the respondents for a declaration that he was the lawful tenant of the property known as ' Pal mar O it eral do Pr ed io A iv ao ' comprising seven lots on an annual rent of Rs . 36 00 payable in advance in three instalments and the first installment of 1968 but the owner , defendant No . 2 in collusion with defendant No 1 executed a deed of lease in favour of the latter effective from January 1 , 1968 on the strength whereof defendant No 2 had been paying the rent upto the end of December 1967 without his tenancy having been validly terminated . The plaintiffs case in the plaint was that they were the lawful tenants of the said property and that they had not been dispossessed therefrom till their possession came to be disturbed after the expiry of the lease period . The Trial Court held that the suit was barred on the principle of res judicata and / or constructive res judicata as found in Order 2 Rule 2 ( 3 ) of the Code of Civil Procedure and dismissed the suit . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The question whether the property was demised to the respondent No . 1 was a mixed question of fact and law which could only be decided by the Civil Court . [ 1020 E ] ( ii ) The High Court has rightly held that since the suit is barred on account of the change in law the proper course would be to follow in the facts and circumstances of the case . [ 1021 G H ; 1022 A B ] ( iii ) The effect of the Fifth Amendment may give rise to a situation where the remedy lies entirely under the Act and may have to be taken in the manner prescribed by or under the statute . [ 1023 C D ] ( iv ) The substantive rights of the parties are governed by the provisions of the Act . But the procedure laid down in Order 7 Rules 10 and 10A of the code of Civil procedure is not applicable to the facts of the present case . It is true that the original plaint and the written statement and counsel were unable to en ligh ten us on the actual nature of the pleadings . [ 1024 F ]

The petitioners were engaged in the construction industry . They filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of their fundamental right to have " equal pay for equal work ". Their claim was that they should be paid at least the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen . They also sought regularisation of their services with the benefits of pen sion , gratuity etc . The Corporation contended that the petitioners are entitled to get the benefit of wage revision and dearness allowance under the Employees ' Provident Fund Act , 1952 . It was further contended that there is no discrimination among the same set of employees by the same master in the same establishment . The Court rejected the contention of the Corporation . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the classification made by the Corporation is not reasonable and that the Corporation has no power to fix the rate of wages payable to the workers employed in the establishment or other like industries but has only the power to determine the rates of wages and allowances payable to such workers . Allow ing the petitions , ^ HELD : 1 . The classification made is not unreasonable . There is no distinction between the two sets of employees working in different establishments . The nature of work done cannot be equated with the nature of job . The degree of work performed can be said to be comparable with the work done by the employee concerned . The two jobs by the mere nom en cl ature or by the volume of work discharged cannot be rated as equal . It is not just a comparison of physical activity . It requires the consideration of various dimensions of the job . [ 669 E ] 2 . The principle of " equal salary for equal pay " cannot be invoked in the case of the petitioner . The petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the . The main object of the corporation is to maintain the modern ar ts and craft s and also to national ise handic raft s and hand loom products . The State Government has been conferred with the powers of framing rules regulating the conditions of service of persons appointed to public services . The Rules do not provide for any particular kind of recruitment . The rule of " Equal pay for Equal Work " does not apply to the petitioners . [ 670 C D ] 3 . The concept of equal pay is not merely an abstract doctrine but a well known concept which has its own peculiar features . The philosophy of equality before law and equal protection of laws must be taken into account . The doctrine of equal work has no application to the present case . [ 671 F H ; 672

The appellant claimed a declaration that the said Laksh m amma was the owner of the properties mentioned in the schedule attached to the plaint and as such was entitled only to a life interest in items 1 and 2 . The suit was resisted by respondent 1 on the ground that he had no right to dispose of those properties , but it was contended that the appellant was not entitled to any share in item 3 and that the suit was barred by limitation . Held : ( i ) The High Court was justified in holding that the plaintiff ' s claim for possession against respondent 1 was barred under section 14 of the Indian Limitation Act , 1908 . ( ii ) The trial court was justified by law in decreeing the suit filed by the appellant . ( iii ) The appeal must be allowed and the decree passed by the trial court is set aside . ( iv ) The appellant has been given full opportunity to prove his case before the trial judge . ( v ) The question whether the appellant is entitled to the benefit of section 14 Of the Indian Evidence Act , 1872 , does not arise at all .

The appellants were manufacturers of " Cinema Ar c Carbon s " manufactured by them . They claimed that they had been purchased by persons other than those who ran cin em as or for any other use . The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the goods under consideration were covered by entry No . 4 of the 1st Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act , 1957 and that the sales tax authorities were bound to consider the use which is ordinarily made of the ar c carbon s . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the entry in question links the taxable object with its general or ordinary use . It was further urged that the words " parts thereof " are used in various entries , such as entry No ., 6 of the First Schedule to Andhra Pradesh ( General Sales tax ) Act , 1958 , and the word ' accessories ' in the said entry must be construed accordingly . Held : ( i ) that the expression " parts " in Entry No . 5 of the first schedule of the Andhra State Act , which is a residuary entry , covers only those parts which are capable of being bought and sold for use as an aid or addition ; ( ii ) that even if the goods are not covered by the description in the first Schedule , they cannot be considered to be parts of machinery which are intended to be used in the market ; ( iii ) that in order to attract the provisions of entry No .( 1 ), the term " parts ", in relation to " articles " would have reference only to those parts of the same article which are meant for use in the construction of the roads , bridges etc . and that these items could also be included in the definition of " parts ".

The petitioners in these petitions were lessees of certain minerals situated within the State of Gujarat . They filed applications for grant of prospecting licences and mining leases under the Bombay Minor Mineral Rules , 1966 . The Government of Gujarat by a notification dated June 26 , 1985 issued under section 15 ( 1 ) of the Act amended the Gujarat Minor Mineral rules 1966 , which was published in the Official Gazette on July 4 , 1986 . By another notification dated August 23 , 1987 the Government of India declared that the mining lease granted to the petitioners shall be deemed to have been granted for one year from the date of commencement of the Rajasthan Minor Mineral Rule 1966 , subject to the condition that the petitioners would pay royalty at the rate of Rs . 50 per metric ton ne by way of royalty . The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notifications before this Court by filing writ petitions contending that the provisions of the aforesaid Act are ultra vires Articles 14 and 19 ( 1 )( f ) and ( g ) of Constitution of India as they violate Article 301 of the Constitution . It was also contended that the impugned notifications were violative of article 300 A of the constitution inasmuch as it infringed the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III of the Constitu tion . Allow ing the petitions , ^ HELD : 1 . No express power can be conferred on an executive fi at or delegate e of any legislature to exercise such powers . [ 409 D ] 2 . The expression " mineral oil " is not defined in the Act but only includes minerals other than mineral oils . The term " mineral ' is defined as including all minerals except mineral oils and minerals . The definition of " mineral ", as given in section 2 ( h ), defines " mineral ". The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Seng un atha Mudali ar of Manj ak oll ai village at a meeting held on June 27 , 1957 . On June 27 the temple was declared as an " exempted " temple under section 6 ( 9 ) of Madras Act 1 of 1925 . The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that the trustees hip of the temple had been not hereditary . The Subordinate Judge passed an order holding that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of the section . In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that there was no hereditary trustee in the temple and that the suit was barred by limitation . Held : ( i ) The definition of ' hereditary trustee ' in section 2 ( c ) of the Madras Act is identical with the word ' heir '. The expression ' hereditary ' has been defined in section 3 ( e ) of Act No . I of 19 11 which means ' any person who holds or may be entitled to receive from his father ' s estate any property or thing whatsoever in respect of which he is entitled to claim such property or anything ; but does not include a person who is a member of the family of a deceased person . The definition includes three types of cases : ( 1 ) succession to the office of the manager of a religious institution succession to which the provisions of the Act apply ; ( 2 ) succession of the holder of the office to the manager ; ( 3 ) succession in the office where the office is held ; ( 4 ) succession being specifically provided for by the f ounder on condition that the scheme of such succession shall cease to operate after the death of the person concerned .

The appellant was tried for the murder of one Vis wanath am Pillai , a village Munsif . On the prayer of the prosecution the case against him was taken up for trial and he was convicted under section 302 / 34 IPC and sentenced to death . He filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed his appeal . In revision the High court acquitted accused but convicted the appellant under section 304 Part II IPC and convicted him under section 120B read with sections 302 and 109 IPC . The High Court acquitted accused on the ground that there was no evidence in support of the first information report . It also held that the conviction and sentence were not sustainable . In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts should have given a liberal interpretation of the provisions of section 300 I . P . C ., as they did not consider the relevant provisions of the Evidence Act and the evidence of the witnesses who had seen the accused running away after the assault is true . Dismis sing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The evidence of this witness does not inspire confidence . There is a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No . 1 in the site plan ( exhibit P 15 ). There are no blood stains on the bench where he was sleeping . [ 709 E ] 2 . The testimony of this un corroborated single eye witness is true and correct . The presence of the deceased near the scene of occurrence is doubtful . The fact that the deceased was last seen alive when the incident took place is not sufficient to hold that the accused was guilty of the offence . [ 710 A B ] 3 . The prosecution has failed to prove that the appellant was actually present at the time of the incident . The police officer who conducted the inquest over the dead bodies of the accused , has clearly stated that the injuries sustained by the deceased could be caused by a sharp edged weapon . The post mortem notes show that the cause of death was due to shock and haemor rhage as a result of ante mortem injury . The doctor has categorically stated that all the injuries were possible by a blunt object . The medical evidence shows that the death occurred within seven years of the marriage . The injuries found on the person of the victim could be inflicted by a knife or a sword . The Doctor has further stated that if the statement of PW 4 is to be believed , the crow d had gathered at the place of occurrence already when he arrived . The Andhra Pradesh Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment ( Require ment as to Res idence ) Act , 1957 for domic iles of Tel eng ana and Tel eng na . The petitioners were employed in various offices located in the States of Hyderabad and Secunderabad . On January 19 , 1969 , le aders of all political parties in the Legislature of the State appeared to have met and reached the decision that to Implement what are called Tel eng aya langu ages will be immediately relieved from service . They also reported that they had been appointed either directly by direct recruitment or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra State . The Government of Andhra Pradesh then passed an order on February 28 , 1969 relieving the petitioners from service with effect from February 28 70 . The respondents challenged this order before the Supreme Court . The Supreme Court dismissed the petition holding that the order was not binding on them and that the petitioners were entitled to protection under article 32 ( 1 )( b ). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned orders were violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the provisions of the Act did not provide for any such protection . [ 117 C ] 2 . It is well settled that the power to make rules is subject to the provisions contained in the Act itself . The Rules made thereunder do not confer any right on the petitioners to claim protection under Articles 14 and 21 of the constitution . [ 118 D E ] 3 . The definition of ' any condition ' in the Rules does not contemplate any particular form of application . The term ' any qualification ' is defined in the Rule to mean any qualification prescribed by the Rules . [ 120 H ; 121 A B ] 5 . The appellant was convicted under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act , 1898 ( VI of 1898 ) and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year in each case . He filed an appeal against his conviction and sentence before the High Court which dismissed his appeal on the ground that he had secre ted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and acquitted him . In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove that these articles were stolen property and that they were not smuggled goods within the meaning of section 2 ( 1 )( d ) of the Prevention of Corruption Act , 1947 . Held : ( i ) that the evidence adduced by the prosecution did not establish that these items were stolen properties but that the appellant had trans formed them from the very same property in which the deceased was residing ; ( ii ) that there was no evidence to show that the ornaments belonging to the father were stolen or that the accused had taken away those ornaments at any time after the incident ; ( iii ) that even if the ornaments belonged to the mother , the presumption would be that the said ornaments were stolen and that the gold ornaments were purchased by the father ' s brother and therefore the presumption could not be drawn against the appellant .

The appellants were convicted under section 85 of the U . P . Panchayat Raj Act , 1947 and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs . 1 , 000 / and further directed that in case of default they shall undergo simple imprisonment for two weeks . The High Court held that the Sarpanch and the Pan ch as had knowledge of the order of stay passed by it staying proceedings pending before them . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The Panch as are not well ver sed in law and procedure and the records maintained by them should not be judged in the same manner as that of ordinary courts . [ 117 B ] ( ii ) The High court was wrong in holding that the Panch as were not well enough to depose before it . It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof , but a judicial officer cannot be made liable for any act done by him or his agent without giving an opportunity to the party concerned to show cause against the proposed action . [ 118 C D ] ( iii ) There is no evidence on record that any such application was made after the proceedings on that date had commenced and evidence taken . [ 119 F ]

The appellant was tried for the murder of Sheo Sahai and his conviction under section 302 , I . P . C ., by the Sessions Judge , Etawah , was confirmed by the High Court . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the entire report of the Ser ologist regarding the death of Sheo Dayal was inadmissible in evidence as its contents were not proved . Held : ( i ) The evidence of the prosecution witnesses was reliable and trustworthy ; ( ii ) the circumstances relied upon by the trial court were not sufficient to convict the accused . The evidence led by the prosecution consisted of the evidence relating to motive , the recovery of sword at the instance of the accused and the circumstance that the accused had a quarrel with the deceased and that the knife used to be used for committing the murder . The extra judicial confession made by the appellant to the Police Officer was admissible in evidence under section 32 of the Indian Evidence Act , 1872 . The fact that the appellant did purchase a sword at night from the place where he was living would not make him an accomplic e but only a person who is said to have seen the occurrence . It could not be held that the weapon used to run away from the scene of occurrence was not recovered from the house or any other place . The mere fact that some one else was present at the time when the appellant took the pistol into possession does not lead to the conclusion that the chain of circumstances was complete . The entire report must show that the intention was to cause the death .

The appellants were elected to the Municipal Corporation of Raipur in the month of December , 1978 under Rule 4 ( 1 ) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities ( Election of Councill ors and Members ) Rules , 1963 . They filed their nominations for election to the municipal corporation of Raipur on November 16 , 1978 . They claimed that they had been included in the electoral roll of the Municipal Council of Raipur as a result of an error in the notice issued by the Returning Officer under Rule 3 ( 2 )( b ) of Madhya Pradesh M unic i mi nal Pal Corporation ( Prepar ation , Revision and Publication of Electoral Ro lls and Selection of Councill ers ) Rules 1966 . They also prayed for the issue of an interim order staying the poll which had explanation at the time of filing of the petition till December 28 , 1978 , and for a direction to the respondents to refrain from conducting the poll on December 31 , 1978 in all the 44 constituencies : Held , that the High Court was right in holding that the appellants had not made out any case for interference with the election process . It is well settled that the power of the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution is discretionary and if there be any doubt or dispute about the correctness of the notice served upon them , it would be open to the High court to interfere with such proceedings .

The first respondent company and its directors were prosecuted for failure to disclose the true facts of their business . They filed a complaint against the first respondent Company and its Directors alleging that they had committed offences under sections 76 , 153 A and 234 I . P . C . and section 164 ( 1 ) of the Companies Act , 1913 , for breach es of sections 20 and 21 of the , which are punishable under section 19 of the Indian Penal Code . The High Court held that the first Respondent was guilty of an offence under section 135 ( 3 ) of that Act and sentenced him to imprisonment for three years and also directed the appellant to pay compensation in accordance with the provisions of section 165 of the Act . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the second respondent was not liable under section 169 of the . It was further urged that the order of acquittal passed by the Presidency Magistrate was erroneous as the High Court had set aside the conviction and sentence of the accused persons . HELD : ( i ) Section 239 of the did not apply to cases where the accused person relies on his default and plead his innocence . [ 412 B ] ( ii ) The question whether there was any contravention of section 239 or section 238 is one of fact depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case . If the accused pleads his guilt , he must be given an opportunity to rebut the presumption . But if he fails to do so , the burden shifts to the accused to prove the charge . [ 413 E F ] ( iii ) The expression " any other offence " used in section 170 does not mean any act done by the accused but includes any act or omission amounting to an offence . The word " any " means something more than mere knowledge . It is clear from the definition of " any offence ". The word ' any ' means anything done by someone else in pursuance of a contract or otherwise . The words " any such thing " cannot be construed as meaning any act performed by anyone else in furtherance of the object of the statute . [ 414 D E ]

The appellant was appointed as a Professor of Radi other apy in the Central Health Service . He was also required to man posts in the Union Territories and the various autonomous bodies . In exercise of the powers conferred by proviso to Art . 309 of the Constitution , the President on May 1 , 1963 made the Central Government ' s order dated May 1 ., 1963 , which came into force 18 on May 5 , 1963 . R . 3 provided that no person who has been working for more than six years in that scale shall be eligible for appointment or promotion as Professor of Medic are from the State Government service unless he is qualified for appointment to the post of Professor of Medicine . The appellant challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court contending that the order of the President was violative of article 14 of the constitution inasmuch as it did not contain any provision for reservation of appointments or posts in favour of persons holding the post in the senior scale . The High Court dismissed the petition . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : ( i ) The power to relax the qualifications is subject to the provisions of the statute . [ 80 G ] ( ii ) The word " prescribed " in r . 8 ( 2A ) means a minimum of three years experience in the field of medicine and a degree in medicine . There cannot be two classes of persons , one being a teaching staff and another being a non teaching staff . [ 81 F ] ( iii ) The expression " prescribed qualification " in cl . ( 2 ) of r . 4 of the Central Medical Services Rules , 1963 does not include a post included in the junior scale without changing the designation of the post . It is for the Union Public Service Commission to adverti se the post as indicated in r .( 2 ). [ 82 E ]

The workmen of the Company , who were working in the factory and whose wages were less than Rs . 2 , 000 per month , were brought up in this Court by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal , Orissa , which was confirmed by the High Court . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had committed an error in determining the minimum wage fixed by the Tribunal as a basis for fixing the minimum wages payable to the employees in respect of their work done during the period between 1962 63 and 1964 64 , and that the Labour Court had erred in not considering the question whether there was any discrimination or ine quality in fixing the maximum wages at the rate of three months ' basic wages , while the case of some clerical staff was based on the circumstances that according to them the bonus should be paid only at the rates prescribed under the Minimum Wages Act , 1948 , and the Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only after giving notice to all concerned including the parties . Held : ( i ) The Tribunal was right in holding that there was no justification for adding dearness allowance to the minimum rates of wages fixed by it in the Award . The principle of industry cum region has been applied by this Court in the case Of Fr ench Motor Car Co . Ltd ., vs Workmen , ; , followed .

The assessee was assessed to tax for the assessment year 1960 61 . In the assessment years 1960 61 and 1959 62 , the Income Tax Officer had issued to him a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act , 1961 . The material portion of that notice reads as follows " Notice under section 147 ( 1 ) of the Income tax act , 1961 ". The assessee ' s total income was assessed at Rs . 69 , 886 / . On June 3 , 1966 , the 1st respondent filed a statement showing various creditors from whom it had borrowed on H un dis during the accounting year in question . In this statement it gave the l ull names and address of the alleged creditors . After enquiry , the assessee ' S firm submitted its income tax return . The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the impugned notice was invalid because it did not comply with the requirements of section 151 ( 2 ) of Income tax . The High Court dismissed the appeal . In appeal by special leave , HELD : ( i ) The Commissioner has mechanically granted permission . He did not himself record that he was satisfied that there were reasons to issue , notice under Section 148 . [ 146 D ] ( ii ) The order of the High Court is set aside and the case remanded to the assessing officer for fresh consideration . [ 147 E F ] ( iii ) The report submitted by the Income - tax Officer to the Commissioner does not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it was a fit case for the issue of a notice . [ 149 G ]

The appellant was a limited company with effect from November 13 , 1947 . The firm was assessed to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50 . The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim of the assessee on the ground that it had transferred its business to a limited Company with effect either from November 1 , 1947 or February 13 , 1948 by an instrument executed on February 7 , 1948 . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was not entitled to relief under section 25 ( 4 ) Of the Indian Income tax Act , 1922 , because the transfer of its business was discontinued in view of the provisions of section 26 ( 2 ). In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) Section 26 ( 3 ) of the In comes Tax Act does not apply when there is no succession to one of such partnership or not . [ 100 C ] ( ii ) The family did not carry on separate business es at each of the five places but had only a number of branches at those places of the same business and in order that there may be a succession to another business . [ 101 D E ] ( iii ) There is nothing in law to prevent common partners constituting two distinct firms in respect of different business es carried on by them for the purpose of the Indian In come tax Act . It is also possible that there might be a series of branches where the business could be trans acted . The appellant , a company registered under the Indian Companies Act 1913 , was a " commercial establishment " within the meaning of section 2 ( 5 ) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act , 1954 . The primary objects of the Federation as set out in its Memorandum of Association were " to promote the business of the firm ". The object of the Union was to provide for an industrial establishment for the benefit of the members of the public and to secure the interests of the general public . In order that the said object should be so provided , it was felt necessary to make arrangements for the spread of commercial and social activities and to provide facilities for the working of the industry . It was also decided by the Government that the provisions of the Act would not apply to the undertaking of the association which had been established for the purpose of carrying on the business or trade of the Association . The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned judgment . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was a commercial establishment within the definition of Section 2 ( 1 )( f ) of Delhi Shops & Establishments Act . The appeal was allowed . On appeal by certificate the High court held that the expression ' trade or business ' in section 11 of the said Act did not include any activity carried on by the appellant but only incidental to the main object of making the Act applicable to the establishment of the respondent . The State appealed to this Court . Held : ( i ) The word " trade " in section 2 is wide enough to include all activities carried on in the course of trade or profession ; ( ii ) The words " trade or Business " do not necessarily mean anything by which one person may be able to carry on his trade or occupation , but merely means something by which another person may not be able either to carry out the trade or use it for some other purpose . The word ' trade ' does not necessarily imply something by whatever name called . The dictionary meaning of the word ' commerce ' is " trade , business or profession " and the word " manufacture " in the context means bringing about any change in the substance of the commodity or goods . The expression " trade ", therefore , cannot be construed in a narrow sense . The question whether the activity of the appellant amounts to " trade ". must depend upon the intention of the legislature . If the words " dealing with " are used in the same sense , they will have to be read as " trade ." The word ` trade ' has not been defined in the Act .

The respondent purchased a business carried on by the appellant as defined in the Madras General Sales Tax Act , 1939 . The assessee paid certain amounts towards sales tax due from him to the transferor and paid some amounts towards the sales tax so determined but there remained some arrears of sales tax payable for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50 . The Sales tax authorities demanded the purchaser of the business from the transferee and also to the State Government for recovery of the amount of sales Tax . The Commercial Tax Officer held that the transaction was not one between the transferor or the transferee but between the transferee . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Commercial Tax officer . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the orders of the appellate authority under section 19 ( 1 ) of the Act . Held : ( i ) The expression " liability " used in the definition of " liability ", in the context of the provisions of the Madras Sales Tax Acts , 1939 , is wide enough to include all liabilities including the liability incurred by the seller in respect of such business and any other liability which may be incurred by him in respect thereof . Held : ( i ) that the High Court was right in holding that there was no jurisdiction to entertain the suit ; ( ii ) that even if the agreement was not enforceable , the same could not be regarded as a case decided within the meaning of section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act , 1872 , and ( iii ) that since the agreement itself provided for a special procedure for obtaining and continuing the sale , the agreement must be construed as a whole and not merely a piece of paper or paper which is capable of being used for any purpose whatsoever . The appellant was a workman in the respondent ' s establishment . The Labour Court held that the termination of his services amounted to retrenchment within the meaning of section 2 ( vi ) of the , and directed payment of compensation . Held : ( 1 ) that the provisions of section 15 were applicable only when an industrial dispute arose between the employer and his employees and that the question whether the workmen were entitled to receive gratuity or not was a mixed question of fact and law and so the Industrial Tribunal was right in holding that the application made by the respondents was incompetent under section 2 . ( 2 ) that section 15 is inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by the Industrial Disputes Act , 1947 .

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department , Pep su . He was charged with criminal misappropriation and forgery of his signature on the acquit tance roll . In the roll for April 1951 one Par ma was mentioned as a kh al asi ( men ial servant ). The case of the prosecution was that there was no person of the name of Par ma to whom the money was entrusted by him . The First Class Magistrate held that the thumb impression found in the acquittal s of the accused were sufficient . On appeal the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed against the appellant . Held , that the conviction of the appellant was illegal . The conviction was illegal because it was not proved that he had been paid Rs . 51 and misappropriated the same . The evidence showed that the appellant received two sums of money from the treasury and handed them over to the em plo y ees . The first sum of Rs . 50 was the amount which was given to the appellant by the police to the im pu g ne d son of Par ama . The second sum of the sum of money was the payment made by the appellant to the sup porters of the money . The third sum of this sum was the money which was taken away by the appe l l ant . The appellant received the sum from the Treasury and the recovery was effected . The High Court was right in holding that the act committed by the accused was an offence punishable under section 465 of the Indian Penal Code .

The appellants were partners of a firm . They had for a long time business relations with a firm known as Bhoj aji Sob ha chand , who was an employee in the appellant firm . In the books of account of the appellants it was shown that the amounts received by them from the Bombay firm were not loans made in the ordinary course of the money lending business and they were paid to the Bombay Firm at the foot of their running account as a bad debt written off as ir recoverable . The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim holding that : ( 1 ) the transactions were mere financing of the funds of the assessee company ; ( 2 ) the payments made to the Madras firm were in fact not loans taken out of the profits of the business of the assessees ; ( 3 ) the amounts were credited to the Calcutta firm ' s account only when the last of such deposits was sent to it before the firm coll apsed in about April 1952 ; and ( 4 ) the amount was allowed to be deducted on the basis of the total receipts of the Bombay partner during the year ending March 31 , 1953 . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Tribunal . On appeal by special leave , the High Court held that : " The finding of the tribunal that the monies sent by the assessee to the Delhi firm were loan made in ordinary course or in respect of any other business of profit is erroneous . It is true that the Tribunal has found that the moneys sent by it were not loan made but were repaid to the principal debtor . But this finding does not mean that the sums in question were not borrowed from the principal borrower . The Tribunal also observed that the amount in question was not debited to the Hyderabad firm ' A ' and therefore the amounts could not be treated as loan made by the principal . The High Court further held that the sum in question did not represent the amount of Rs . 2 , 68 , 385 / which was the interest payable under section 10 B of the Indian Income Tax Act , 1922 . Held , that the findings reached by the Tribunal are findings of fact and those findings are supported by evidence on record . The conclusion arrived at by the tribunal is not supported by proper discussion of the material before it . It cannot be denied that the conclusions reached by it are findings or findings of facts . The finding recorded by the court is binding on this Court .

They filed a complaint against the respondent No . 1 under section 31 ( 1 ) read with section 33 of the , and also under section 33 ( 1 )( b ) of the Act alleging that they had committed offences punishable under sections 31 ( i ), 32 ( 2 ) and 33 ( 3 ) of t he , and section 33 A of the . The Chief Presidency Magistrate acquitted all the accused including the appellants but convicted them under section 30 ( 1 ). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as the conciliation proceedings could not be said to have concluded in the case where no settlement is arrived at , the appellants should be held guilty under section 12 ( 6 ) of that Act . HELD : ( i ) Section 12 ( 5 ) of 1947 provides for the submission of report by the Conciliation Officer within 14 days from the date of receipt of the report by him . It is true that section 12 of 1947 empowers the State Government to make an order directing the inquiry into any matter referred to in section 10 or section 11 of the 1946 Act . But section 12 does not contemplate that the report must be made and the proceedings closed after 15 days . [ 739 D ] ( ii ) The provisions of sub section 2 ( b ) are mandatory and do not support the contention of the appellant that the inquiry should be deemed to have commenced when the report is received by the appropriate Government . The termination of the conciliation proceeding can only be done if there is a settlement between the parties or if the conciliation officer does not make his report within 14 months . [ 741 E F ]

The petitioner was detained under section 3 ( 2 ) of the , and he was ordered to be set at liberty . He was also placed under preventive detention in connection with a case registered against him . In this case , on 24 . 12 . 1985 , between 10 and 10 . 30 . A . M ., the detenu was arrested by the police officer and his associates who were there along with others . On the basis of the aforesaid criminal cases , the detaining authority found that the detenu had been in custody of the police force and therefore , he was required to be detained under the Act . The grounds as mentioned in the order of detention were served upon the detenu on the same day i . e . on 25 . 1 . 1986 . The detenu was released on bail on 18 . 2 . 86 . Thereafter , the detenu filed an application before the District Magistrate for release of the detenu from jail on the ground that the Detaining Authority had not considered the fact that the said detenu was in custody and that the possibility of his release would be very bleak . The State Government rejected the said application on the sole ground that it was not possible to consider the question whether the detenu could be released or not . The High Court held that the order passed by the District magistrate was vitiated because the detenu ' s activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order . It further held that since the order was passed without any proper consideration , the service of the order must have been made good by the detaining authorities . The appellant preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court which was dismissed . Hence the present appeal by special leave . Allow ing the Appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The order of preventive detention is not justified if it is based on no cogent material . [ 908 D ] 2 . The power of preventive Detention given to the appropriate authority must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated by the various provisions of the different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection . There must be awareness of the facts conducive to the protection of the fundamental freedom s of our citizens . If a man is in custody , there can be no imminent possibility of being released , the power of detention will not be exercised . [ 909 F G ] 3 . The mere fact that a person may be released on parole does not mean that the detaining Authority has to apply its mind to the question as to whether the person is likely to be released . The satisfaction of the detaining au th ro ity is not subjective but depends able on the circumstances of each particular case

The appellant firm was a dealer in gold trade , i . e ., manufacturers of gold and silver . The respondents were engaged in the gold business as money lenders . They were purchasing goods from the market for their personal use and were also selling them to the customers . The High Court held that section 28 ( 6 ) of the Act did not provide for any guideline or guide lines by which the Administrator could refuse permission or grant permission . On appeal by the Union of India it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the power conferred upon the Administrator under section 28 of the Gold Control Act should be exercised only when there is an express provision in the statute itself prohibiting the exercise of such discretion . Held : ( 1 ) that the legislature has used the words " may " in cl . ( b ) of sub s .( 2 ) of S . 28 of Indian Income tax Act , 1922 , while defining the word ' area ' in cl s . ( d ), ( f ) and ( g ) of s . 28 ( 3 ) of Indian In com et ax Act , 18 64 , and the expression " specified area " in r . ( 4 ) of cl . 2 of the Schedule to the Act must mean the area within which the applicant is required to carry on his business as such dealer . It is clear from the language of cl s .( d ) and cl . 5 of the schedule to the Indian Income Tax Act that the Legislature intended to give wide powers to the Administrator with respect to certain matters relating to the business of the assessee . The expression " prescribed period " in the proviso to cl . 3 of the said Schedule means the period during which the application is made and not the period of limitation provided for in the said proviso . [ 10 E F ] ( 2 ) The object of the legislation is to prevent exploitation of persons who are likely to be adversely affected by the proposed action of the Administrator . The Administrator is given limited authority or power to refuse permission to carry out the purposes of the enactment . The power to reject the application depends on the nature of the subject matter involved in the case . The scope of the power is wider than the power to accept the application . The legislative intent behind the rule is that the Administrator can delegate its power to the Commissioner if he is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to do so . The rule making power is discretionary in character and is not arbitrary but is based on sound principles . The test of reasonableness is whether the particular circumstances have been taken into account and

The appellants , who were the trustees of a temple , filed an application before the District Munsif for possession of certain properties in suit . They claimed that they had been granted in Inam to the ancest ors of one Ambal ath ad um Pach ai Uday avar and his son Am ri th aling a ly er , Chinn asamy Iyer and Rang araj a Red diar . The trial court held that the alien or was still alive and that the property in question belonged to the temple ; and so , it was not liable to be partitioned between the two parties . On appeal by special leave , the High Court set aside the decree passed by the lower appellate Court and restored that of the trial Judge . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( 1 ) The contention that the properties in dispute were not given to the father of the appellant as he was the manager of the temple is not correct . [ 10 E ] ( 2 ) The mere fact that the original grant ee was appointed as trustee does not mean that the person who was appointed under the will has no right to continue in possession of the properties . It is only when the original assignee was appointed by respondent No . 4 that the said assignment would have been made on behalf of the deity . If that be so , there is nothing wrong in the finding of the courts below that more than 12 years had elapsed since the date of the removal of the previous manager . [ 11 F G ] ( 3 ) The evidence shows that the assig nor was a hereditary trustee and the management had been taken over by other persons who are acting as de facto man agers of the trust . There is no reason why the High court should not have considered the matter from any angle . [ 13 H ; 14 A B ]

The appellant , a partnership firm , was granted licence to construct a cinema Hall at the proposed site . On July 22 , 1966 , the Secretary of the District Magistrate issued a notice under section 3 ( 1 ) of the Jammu and Kashmir ( Cin emato graph ) Act , 1989 calling upon the appellant to show cause why he should not be suspended as he had failed to comply with the terms of the said notice . The appellant filed an appeal against the order passed by the District magistrate in C . M . P . No . 454 of 1981 . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned order was violative of principles of natural justice inasmuch as it did not contain any reasons for quashing the order . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The power to suspend a licence is conferred only by Section 6 F of the Act . [ 579 E ] ( ii ) The District Magistrate has no jurisdiction to pass the impugned orders . The learned Single Judge has rightly held that the District Collector had no authority to suspend the licence . [ 580 B ] ( iii ) The order of the Division Bench cannot be sustained on the facts and circumstances of the case . [ 578 D ]

The appellants were displaced persons , and on their death the respondent entered into an agreement with them for a period of five years on 12 9 1951 . On 30 8 1952 the respondent executed a lease deed in favour of the appellants for a term of 5 years on the terms and conditions set out therein . In pursuance of this agreement the appellants had to pay Rs . 1 , 000 per month as rent for the said premises . The appellants filed a suit against the respondent for possession of the mills and factory and the factory in question . The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants were entitled to the protection of section 12 ( 1 ) of the Act . The High Court held that the notice was not valid because it did not contain any clause which expressly provided that the lessee shall be deemed to have been given the right to terminate the tenancy if he failed to do so within three months from the date of the notice . Held , that the respondent was acting within his authority in issuing Exhibit C in respect of the lands in dispute and therefore the appellants could not be evicted under section 12 of the . The effect of the execution of Exhibit C is that the lessor ' s rights are extinguished by virtue of the provisions of section 18 of the , and that the respondents were bound to comply with the requirements of section 19 of the and they cannot be dispossessed without complying with the provisions contained in section 18 . It is true that the words " or otherwise " used in section 2 ( c ) must mean " or " and " and not " but only " and that " or ". But there is no such provision in the Act which authorises the Custodian to cancel the lease . The word " or ", in the context , means " or "; and " includes " and does not include " or ," and " does not mean " and includes " or '. " and the word " and ".

The appellant , who was the father of a minor son of Raghubir Singh and used to study in Punjab and further held that he was a major son of Kuldip Singh . He had been declared as a minor by the Board of Revenue for Rajasthan and his son Sur end rap al Singh through his next friend Shri Jagjit Singh , maternal grand mother of the minor . The Sub Divisional Officer , Hanum angarh passed an order on 10th August , 1972 holding that the father and the son constitute two separate units and each one of them was entitled to get 62 Big has and 16 Biswas . It was also held that the land in possession of the appellant was ancestral . The sub Divisional Officer after considering the evidence and hearing both the parties confirmed the order of the Sub Divisional officer and remanded the case to the Sub divisional Officer for de novo determination of ceiling area for the appellant in law . In pursuance of the direction of the Board , the Sub Division Officer , after giving opportunity to the appellant to file written statement and cross examination of the witnesses , allowed the application filed by the appellant under Section 230 of the Code of Criminal Procedure , 1973 ( hereinafter referred to as ' the Code ') and directed the Sub - Divisional Officer to decide the matter afresh within three months from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment . The appellant preferred revision petition before the Board which was dismissed by the High Court . Hence this appeal by special leave . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . A similar question arose before the Rajasthan High Court in K ana and others vs Board of revenue , Rajasthan , ; , decided on 19th July , 1979 , followed .

The appellant was a journal ist and the 1st respondent engaged in the production or publication of newspapers . The 1st respondent had been working as an advocate for the first respondent . The 2nd respondent was employed by the appellant on a daily wage basis . The appellant ' s services were terminated by the 1st Respondent , who was not a practising advocate . The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to the benefits conferred upon him under the Act . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the service rendered by the 2nd respondent amounted to " newspaper " within the meaning of section 2 ( c ) of the Act and therefore the appellant could not be said to have been appointed as an Advocate . Dismis sing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The expression " newspaper ", as defined in the Act means any printed periodical work containing public news or comments on public news and includes such other class of news or comment aries which are published in some newspaper . [ 779 B ] 2 . The word " newspaper ' is used in the definition of newspaper . It does not mean any person who is employed either directly or indirectly in a supervisory capacity , or being employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity , performing , whether in part or in full time employment in a judicial capacity . [ 780 C D ] 3 . The words " newspaper establishment " in the context of the definition in section 2 of the Advocates Act , 1961 , read with section 2 , of the said Act , do not include any such person who has been appointed by the Central Government as an agent of the State Government . [ 791 E F ] 4 . Section 2 ( f ) of Act provides that every newspaper establishment shall be deemed to be a newspaper establishment . [ 792 G H ; 792 A ]

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises . He had been described as the licensee and the respondent had been styled as the licen sor . The appellant continued by virtue of that agreement . It is alleged that this agreement was entered into between the parties since the respondent wanted to charge more rent or mesne profits . This agreement was executed on 9th February , 1965 . The main contention raised in this appeal was whether the appellant was an ' occupier ' within the meaning of section 2 ( 1 )( d ) of the Bombay Rent Act , 1947 . The High Court held that the appellant had not been able to prove that he was a tenant or a licensee . On appeal , the Division Bench held that there was no estoppel against the appellant . In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the view taken by the High Court or the Court of Small Causes was incorrect . Dismis sing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The view taken in the case of Satyanarayan Lax am in arayan Hegde & Ors . vs Mallikar jun Bhavan appa Tir um ale , A . I . R . 1960 S . C . 137 , followed .

The respondent was a resident of the former State of Rajasthan . He applied for and obtained a permit for export of 15 , 000 ma unds of ch uni from the former Dholpur State on June 28 , 1947 and remained in force upto December 2 , 1947 . On July 1 , 1947 the United State of Jaipur passed the Rajasthan Excise Duties Ordinance 1949 which provided that no liquor shall be exported from the latter State until the expiry of six months after the date of its issue or before the commencement of the Rajasthan excise Duties Ordinance , 1949 . The appellant filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution claiming refund of the excess amount paid to him as duty on the ground that he had not been granted any licence for export ation of the goods . The High Court held that the agreement did not confer any right on the appellant to claim refund of excess amount but only the right to claim rebate and that the contract was void because it was made by the Rul er of Jodhpur and therefore the agreement could not be said to have been recognised by the new sovereign . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The agreement was not a law within the meaning of article 286 of the Co ven ant . [ 184 D ] ( ii ) The terms of the agreement were not intended to be implied unless there was anything repugnant in the subject or context . It is clear from the language of the document that the terms of a statute are not necessarily implied . There can be no question of recognition by the Union of India . [ 185 G H ; 186 A B ] ( iii ) The expression " in accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Act " has to be read in the light of the context in which they appear . If the intention of the legislature was to exclude the exemption from income tax and excise duty , then the exemption would be available if the conditions laid down therein were satisfied . [ 187 C E ]

The appellants were the traders in cotton and ground nut . They purchased certain agricultural produce from the market committee at Koil patti , which was a stock broker . On February 25 , 1952 , the State Government issued G . 0 No . 251 ( Food & Agriculture Department ) directing that all the traders who failed to take out licences as provided therein should pay sales tax on the purchase price of the commodity purchased by them . The appellants challenged the validity of the said G . O . before the High Court contending that the levy of sales tax under section 14 of the Act was illegal because it did not fall within the terms of the Explanation to section 14 ( 1 )( b ). Held : ( i ) that the expression ' sale ' in the context of the definition of " trade allowance " in section 2 ( f ) of the Madras Commercial Crop s Markets Act , 1951 , must be construed in its ordinary sense and if there is any doubt about the meaning of the words used in the definition , the same would be repugnant to the object of the legislation ; ( ii ) that even though the word ' sale ', in the present case , means something given as compensation for the use of the property or goods sold , it would not mean that the legislature intended to exclude the sale of such property from the purview of the term ' sale '.

The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code . The High Court , in appeal , held that the conviction s could not be maintained but was of opinion that the sentence in each case should be commuted to transportation for life . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the sentences in each of these cases should be reduced to transportation in all five cases . Held , ( i ) that the words " imprisonment for life " in section 304 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must mean imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years or with fine or both . It is well settled that where an offence is committed by a person who has been convicted of an offence and sentenced him to death , he would be liable to pay compensation if he had not been found guilty of any offence . But when the offence is proved against him , the sentence of death can be imposed only if there are compelling reasons for doing so . If the sentence is not passed without proper consideration , the accused will have to suffer the consequences of his act . The word ' imprisonment ' in section 300 of the Criminal Procedure Code means imprisonment for the term of imprisonment for one year . [ 54 C D ]

The petitioner was appointed as a Section Officer under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India . He was compulsorily retired by order dated 3 . 8 . 1976 with effect from 5 . 11 . 1976 made under Rule 56 ( j ) of Fundamental Rules . He challenged his removal on the ground that he had been prematurely retired by an order dated 4 . 9 . 1967 without any notice to him , and that the impugned order was contrary to the express provisions of FR 56 ( jj )( i ) and Article 311 ( 2 ) of the Constitution . The writ petition was allowed by this Court holding that the petitioner was entitled to payment of salary and allowances admissible to him for the period between 5 . 1 . 1976 and 29 . 2 . 1980 when he was compulsorily retire . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the ratio of the decision in Tah ili ani ' s case is not correct and sub clause ( ii ) of Rule 56 of the Fundamental Rules would apply only if the employee concerned has completed more than one year of service before attaining the age of fifty years . Dismis sing the appeals , ^ HELD : 1 . The ratio of a decision in Ta ili ani vs State of Bihar , [ 1981 ] 1 SLR 935 , relied upon by the petitioner , will be applicable to the present case since the petitioner had already attained the age o f superannuation . [ 112 E F ] 2 . The petitioner would have superannuated from service on 29 . 02 . 1980 if he had not been compulsorily retired with effect therefrom . But he would have retired from service after 29 . 12 . 1980 . If the petitioner would still have retired , he would be entitled to pension and other benefits admissible under the rules . [ 113 G H ; 114 A B ] 3 . The principle of " no work no pay " applies to the petitioner because he was an officiating government servant . [ 114 C D ]

The deceased was the husband of respondent No . 1 and father of the respondents No . 2 to 5 , who were the legal heirs of the deceased . The deceased died int estate on 12th January 1961 . He had filled a proposal for insurance for Rs 50 , 000 on 27th December 1960 . The appellant Corporation repudiated his claim on the ground that he had not received any amount in respect of the policy which was issued by it . The High Court held that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Life Insurance Corporation and that the deceased had signed the proposal form as an agent of the appellant Corporation . On appeal by the State Government , the Division Bench held that the LIC had acted in accordance with the terms of the contract and the appellant was entitled to recover the entire sum paid by him from the respondents . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) It is well settled that where a contract of insurance has been made by the parties , the question whether the final acceptance must be communicated to the offer or not would depend merely on the way in which negotiations for an insurance have pro gressed . See in this connection statement of law in Mac G illi vr ay & Par king ton on Insurance Law , Seventh Edition page 94 para 215 . ( ii ) The fact that the life assured had given a proposal to the appellant corporation does not den ote acceptance unless the person making the offer is aware of the same . [ 353 C D ] ( iii ) The High Courts are right in holding that the contract of Insurance is one of utmost good faith and the contract is governed only when the party to whom an offer is made accepts it unconditionally and communic ates his acceptance to the person giving it . [ 354 E F ] ( iv ) The decision of the High Court is correct . [ 355 B ]

The first defendant applied in Suit No . 118 of 1967 for an interim injunction restraining encashment of the letters of credit pending disposal of the suit , and the second defendant filed a suit against the first defendant for recovery of Rs . 1 , 00 , 000 /- on the ground that he had committed certain acts of misconduct by way of fraud or misrepresentation . The High Court held that the first respondent was not entitled to grant of a certificate under article 133 ( 1 )( a ) of the Constitution as it did not comply with the provisions of article 134 ( 1 ) ( a ). In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The order granting ad interim injunction is a final order which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding but only directs the filing of a complaint under section 205 read with section 114 I . P . Code . [ 702 B ] ( ii ) The power conferred upon the court under article 132 ( 1 ), is discretionary and has to be exercised sparingly and only if compelling reasons exist for doing so . It cannot be said that the court has no discretion in the matter . [ 703 C D ] ( iii ) The High Courts have been given powers to pass orders directing the filing or production of documents and giving them opportunity to produce evidence before passing any adverse order . [ 704 E F ] ( iv ) The jurisdiction of the court to entertain a complaint is limited to the question whether the order passed by the High Court is final or not . [ 705 A ]

The assessee was a manufacturer of cotton yarn and the process or . in which he carried on his business , was sold by him to the process ors for processing . The assessee had been paying duty under the Central Excise Act , 1944 . The Central Government issued a notification dated 1st March , 1974 exempt ing the goods manufactured by it from payment of excise duty . The exemption contained in this notification was subject to certain conditions . The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the value of grey cloth in the hands of the process er would be the assessable value of the processed fabric and not the price at which he would be selling the processed fabrics . The Appellate Tribunal upheld the order of the Appellate Authority but allowed the appeal . In the appeal to this Court , it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the sale of the grey cloth amounted to manufacture within the meaning of section 2 ( f ) of the Act and therefore the value should have been included in the price of the finished fabric . Dismis sing the Appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . 1 The expression " deemed " means something more than what is actually used in relation to the manufacture of the final product . [ 345 D ] 2 . 1 It is well settled that when there are two different methods of valuation , one for determination of the value , the other for determining the value and the other , for determining whether the transaction value is the true value of such goods or not , has to be determined having regard to the relevant factors . [ 346 E F ] 3 . 2 The word ' deemed ' means something less than what has been done or omitted to be done . The term ' deemed '. includes anything more than the amount of the duty paid or payable on the excisable goods . [ 347 G H ; 348 A B ]

The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the Panchayat Samiti , Lohar u on June 1 , 1963 . On January 21 , 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk in 1973 and later on promoted as an Assistant Head Clerk on April 1 , 1975 . On March 14 , 1975 a resolution was passed by respondent 3 regular ising the post of Head Clerk . On April 1 ,. 1975 a Resolution was passed appointing the appellant as a head clerk . On May 13 , 1975 the appellant was promoted to the post . On July 13 , 1976 the appellant ' s appointment as a peon was approved by the State Government . In February , 1974 the appellant made a representation that his services should be treated as permanent and that he should be absorbed in the Government service . The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of absorption . A Single Judge of the High court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no right to continue in the service of the Panchayat since he was not entitled to be considered for promotion to the higher post . The Division Bench held that the Panchayat had no power to make appointments to the Panchayats . The appeal was allowed . The High Court held that there was no provision in the Act which dealt with the conditions of service of members of the Gram Panchayat and directed that the services of the appellant be regularised . It further held that if the appellant is aggrieved by his absorption on a lower post , he could have challenged it before the appropriate authority under the Act . The State Government issued a notification dated August 16 , 1977 amending the Punjab Panchayati Raj ( Amendment ) Act , 1973 introducing new provisions in the Punjab Panchayat Samiti s and Zilla Parishads Rules , 1965 . The amendment was brought into force on December 31 , 1978 . The amended section 15 ( 4 ) of the Amending Act provided that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1 ., 1973 shall continue to work on the same terms and conditions on which they were employed by the panchayat Samiti until they were absorbed in Government service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed . The appellants contended that the impugned amendment was ultra vires the Constitution because the appellant did not possess the requisite qualifications for being considered for the post in question .
