The properties in dispute were owned by the Math Sa una or the deity . The temple was constructed on a land of the Math and installed a deity ac claimed by the Mahant Shiv sh ankar Y ati , who executed a wa qf deed on November 12 , 18 92 ded ic ating various properties to the deity with the intention that arrangements for b ho g , deep dan and other expenses be met from them . The chari ties of the math were let out to the idol s of the Temple and the deity was given a right to use it as a place of worship . The deity was also given a share in the property of the deity and the temple was not used as a residence for acquiring further property in the name of the idol . The suit was contested by the appellants contending that the temple had been purchased by the deity for the benefit of the devo tees and the income derived therefrom was not taxable under section 2 ( 1 )( i ) of the U . P . Agricultural Income Tax Act 1948 , but the assessment proceedings were initiated against the deity under section 10 of the Act . Held , that the claim was not accepted by the assessing authority and the High Court was right in holding that the grant of succession certificate by the District Judge was not valid . The mere fact that the amount of Rs . 30 , 000 was paid to the temple by the trustees does not make any difference between the amount received by the temple and the amount which is received by way of donation . The grant of the succession certificate was only for the purpose of recovering the sum spent by the trust . The burden of proof cast on the person claiming exemption from the payment of the estate was upon him . The onus of proving that the property was not ancestral was on him . It was for the person who made the claim to prove the same . The presumption of the character of the property being discharged by the person asserting it to be so , the burden of proving the same was on the party who makes the claim . In the present case , there could be no doubt that the entire property was held by the donor to belong to the Math . But the question whether the property can be said to belong exclusively to the math or the idol is one of fact . The test laid down by this Court in the case of [ Smt . Shanti Devi vs Commissioner of Income tax , Bihar & Orissa ] ; , applied .

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan filed a writ petition before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana challenging the order of the Assistant Custodian on the ground that they had been wrongly fitted in the village Kar o dian . They also challenged the validity of the allotment of seven non residential plots to them by the Assistant Controller , on the grounds ( 1 ) that the allotment was made without any authority or sanction ; ( 2 ) that there was no provision for cancellation of allotment of land in favour of the appellants ; and ( 3 ) that as the appellants were not entitled to allotment of sub urban land at all , their allotments could not be cancelled merely because the notification under section 12 ( 1 ), which provided for cancellation , was issued after the expiry of two years from the date of the publication of the notification . Held , that the appellants did not have locus standi to make out a new case at this stage of argument . It is true that the property , though it might be , transferred to the manager and the same was allotted to him but that does not mean that he was entitled to allot the sub urban plot at all . In the present case , the appellants had no right to challenge the allotment in view of the provisions of section 19 ( 1 ). The only effect of r . 102 is that the land allotted to the appellants was transferable and the appellants ' claim was rejected .

The State Government of Uttar Pradesh issued a notification on May 5 , 1985 inviting applications from eligible candidates for recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari ( Women ) in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale ( Women ' s Branch ). The advertisement was published on May 4 , 1985 and a corrigendum was published by the Public Service Commission on June 8 , 1985 . The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview / personality test . After the written examination and personality test , the Public Services Commission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for re holding of the recruitment examination . On account of improper feeding into the exce l tion process , the High Court cancelled the entire selection process . In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the advertisement inviting applications had been published on the basis of the result of the written test and viva voce test , there was no justification for cancelling the entire process . It was also urged that the High court should have quashed the decision of the Public Selection Com mission rejecting the candidature of the appellant . Dismis sing the appeals , ^ HELD : 1 . The High Court was right in upholding the decision taken by the public authority . [ 125 E ] 2 . The question whether the High Cour t could issue a writ of certiorari or not is a matter which has to be determined by the Court . [ 126 G ] 3 . The power of judicial review under Article 226 of the Constitution of India is very wide and can only be exercised when there is an error apparent on the face of record . [ 127 F ]

The appellant filed a suit for possession of the D era and the properties attached to it . Som Dass died on 13 10 1970 leaving behind him Shi am Dass as his Che la , who was the kar ta of the said D era . The respondent instituted a suit against Som Dass in respect of certain property which had been inherited by him from his father . A decree was passed in favour of Som Dass on the ground that he was not entitled to represent the der a as its duly elected Che la . The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant did not know about the death of Som Parkash but only stated that the respondent was the Che la and that he had no knowledge about the demise of Som Lal . The High Court held that the appeal was incompetent and dismissed the appeal . In appeal by special leave , the appellant contended : ( i ) that the suit was barred by limitation ; ( ii ) that there was no abatement of the appeal even if Som Dass was not impleaded within the period prescribed under Order 22 , rule 10 , and ( iii ) that since the suit had abated and the appeal had abated , the appeal should be allowed . Held , that the question whether the appellant had any knowledge about his death or not could have been decided only after the decision of the case .

The Andhra Pradesh State Legislature in its wisdom , by virtue of the proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution , enacted the Fundamental Rules and the amendments thereto . By G . O . Ms . No . 128 dated April 29 , 1969 , the Governor General was pleased to make certain amendments to the Fundamental Rule as well as the amendment made thereunder . In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso , the Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification on May 24 , 1968 amending the Fundamental rules which provided that all Government servants who had already attained the age of 55 years shall retire from service with effect from February 28 , 1983 . The petitioners contended that they were entitled to continue in service till January 9 , 1983 when the Ordinance was promulgated and that their services could not be terminated without giving them an opportunity of being heard . They also contended that the proviso was ultra vires the Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Articles 14 , 16 ( 1 ) and ( 2 ) of the constitution inasmuch as it infringed the fundamental rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitu tion . Allow ing the Writ Petitions , ^ HELD : ( i ) The power conferred by Article 309 is of a legislative character and is subject to the provisions of the Act . [ 582 B ] ( ii ) The proviso to rule 2 was deleted by the second notification . The proviso was added to rule 3 of the Rules framed under the proviso . It did not contain any provision for the extension of the benefit of the period of service rendered by the employees in the previous year to the date of retirement . The object of the amendment was to provide greater employment opportunities to the employees . [ 583 C D ] ( iii ) The amendment made to the Proviso to rule 4 of the Fundamental Ru es was retrospective and therefore the amendment must have prospective operation . [ 584 E F ] ( iv ) The impugned order cannot be sustained . The contention that the executive , in a given case , has an unfair advantage over those who are in service cannot be accepted . [ 585 H ; 587 A ]

The appellants were dealers in the State of Haryana . They purchased raw materials from manufacturers who sold them out of India and paid tax thereon in terms of section 9 ( 1 ) of the Act . Their sales were made by the assessees to dealers who , in turn , exported those goods out of the country . On these facts , it was claimed that they had no business or any other place within the State and that their purchases were not liable to be taxed under section 9 of the Sales Tax Act . This claim was rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court held that the purchase tax on the raw material was leviable only if the charge under section 3 ( 2 )( a ) was levied at the time when the goods were actually removed from the State to any place outside it otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The purchase tax is payable by the assessee for the purpose of assessment of the raw materials which are received by him as an input in his own factory . [ 347 G ] ( ii ) The question whether the purchase money received by the dealer can be said to have been used for the manufacture of goods for the purposes of assessment is a matter to be decided by the assessing authority and not by the Tribunal . [ 348 D E ] ( iii ) Section 6 will not come into play where the goods are disposed of either directly or through some other source . It does not cover the entire transaction value but merely provides for the payment of the purchase price . [ 349 F ] ( iv ) The expression " turnover " has been defined in section 5 ( 3 ) of C . S . T . Act , 1956 , which includes all taxes , cess es , fees , charges , etc ., which may be levied or collected on the sale of such goods . [ 351 A B ]

The appellants were registered dealers under section 11 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act . They claimed exemption from sales tax in respect of sales of cotton of the total value of Rs . 68 , 493 2 6 and sales of cas tor oil of the aggregate value of about Rs . 6 , 47 , 509 1 6 on the ground that these sales were not carried out by them within six months from the date of purchase by M / s . Daulat ram Rameshwar lal . The goods were sent to an address outside the State of Bombay within a period of six months after the purchase by the appellants . The sellers filed a declaration declaring the goods as " goods " within six weeks from the receipt of the order of assessment . The appellants contended that they had no intention to sell the goods at any time before the goods came into their possession ; that the goods remained their property till the goods had crossed the customs fron tier and therefore the sale was exempt from tax under article 286 ( 1 )( b ) of the Constitution . Held : ( i ) that the expression ' person to whom he has sold the goods " in section 10 ( b ) means " a person who is not a registered dealer " and that the words " a registered trader " are used in the proviso to sub section ( 3 ) of section 8 which provides for the levy of tax on the sale or purchase of goods . The word " a " is wide enough to include a registered person . It does not mean a registered manufacturer but only a registered Dealer . A registered dealer can be said to have purchased goods from another registered dealer if it is found that the purchaser is not registered . In the present case , the seller did not file a declaration in terms of section 4 ( 1 ) of that Act . He could not be regarded as a registered dealers because he had not made a false declaration of his intention to do so . The fact remains that the owner of the goods was not registered as required by section 8 ( b ). [ 927 E F ]

The appellant married the respondent and his children . The first wife was a second wife , who had been divorced by the respondent ' s father . A suit for partition of the property in which the husband had hou sed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes . For some time there was no dispute between the parties . But when the respondent refused to accept this status and asserted that she had not received any legal heir ship certificate from her husband , the appellant filed a suit claiming that she has become the absolute owner of the flat and various deposits in respect of the said flat made with the cooperative housing society . The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had transferred the suit premises to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned . In appeal the High Court held that the transfer of the suit property did not amount to an agreement to sell as contemplated under section 125 ( 3 ) of the Criminal Procedure Code , 1973 . It further held that since the respondent failed to prove that she was still a divorce e , it could not be said that she is entitled to maintenance . Dismis sing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The appellant having entered into a compromise voluntarily without any right or authority cannot claim any benefit thereunder . [ 78 G ] 2 . The respondent had taken a plea that she being a divorce ee , she was not a divorce but a divorce and therefore ineligible for maintenance . She had no locus standi to maintain herself . [ 79 F ] 3 . The fact that the appellant had given up her s oul and had already paid her customary and personal law requirement will not disentitle her from getting maintenance . [ 80 H ; 81 A B ] 4 . The question whether the respondent was a divorce or divorce does not arise at all because the respondent did not have any other income . The expression " marriage " means a contract of marriage . There must be a reasonable relation between the sum so paid and its potential as provision for maintenance and the payment of maintenance . The word " marriage ", in the context of section 127 ( 3 )( b ), is used in the sense of " dissolution of marriage ". The word ' marriage ' is defined in section 2 ( c ) of Hindu Marriage Act , 1955 , to mean a marriage solemnized on or after the commencement of the Hindu Ad options and Maintenance Act , 1956 , and includes a marriage solemn ised before the commencement thereof . Section 2 ( d ) defines " marriage ceremony " to mean an act done by one party to another ,

The appellant , a landlord of a building in the city of Madras , was granted a lease of certain properties under two lease deeds in favour of M / s . India Automobiles , which was then the sole proprietary concern of one of them who had leased out the property to another and was converted later into a partnership concern of G . G . and his four sons . The rent for the premises was Rs . 150 per month . On 30 . 7 . 1953 , all the co owners of the property ( viz ., the appellant ) sold the property on the ground that it was a part of an estate and became the owner thereof by virtue of section 4 of the Act . The appellant filed an application before the Rent Controller under the Act claiming that he should be deemed to have been inducted as a tenant under the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act , 1882 , and that the fair rent claimed was not correct . The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the appellant was entitled to recover the amount from the tenants . In appeal to this Court , HELD : 1 . The High Court has taken the view that the question whether there is a relationship of landlord and tenant or a tenant arises only when the landlord or a person having a share in the land holds a right over such a tenant and the landlord does not acquire any interest in the property . [ 549 E ] 2 . The position cannot be different under section 4 . It would be wrong to read a wider jurisdiction to the Rent contro ller to decide questions of title also . If the civil court in this case had come to the conclusion that there is no relationship of a landlord and a tenant , the Rent Control Act does not provide for a machinery for recovery of the amount . The amount has to be recovered by the landlord only by recourse to a civil court . This gives an indication that the determination of the relationship between the parties is also not conclusive . [ 550 C D ] 3 . Section 4 of Act provides only a mach in ery for fixation of fair rent in respect of certain pre m ises . It is the quantum of fair rents that arise for deter min ation by the Rent Contro ll ers . There is no doubt that , since an application for this purpose can lie only by a landlord or tenant , it will have to pass a decree in favour o the landlord . [ 551 B C ]

The petitioner ' S late employee who was given sufficient opportunity to file his objection to the tentative list was unable to make out any ground for interference with the final select list . [ 10 88 D ] 2 . The list was then prepared . The High Court directed the Central Gover nment to consider the matter afresh . [ 11 89 E F ] 3 . The Union of India vs G . R . Prabha val kar & Ors ., ; , referred to .

The deity of his worship was sh outed by the members of the public and a public religious trust . The idol was then brought to the temple for worship by the devo tees in succession . The deity was then taken over by the trustees , who were present at the time when the ceremony was held . The trustees of the deity had been managing the affairs of the temple . The temple with its properties constituted a public trust under section 2 ( 13 ) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act , 1950 . In view of the provisions of sections 3 and 4 of the Act , the deity was not a public charitable trust within the meaning of section 2 of the Indian Trusts Act . The Assistant Charity Commissioner after requisite notice made an enquiry into the matter in accordance with the provisions contained in section 6 of the Maharashtra Public Trusts Ac commod ation Control Act , 1960 . He also found that the Sansthan was not an endowment property as defined in section 2 . 1 of the said Act . On appeal , the Appellate Tribunal confirmed the decision of the Assistant Charity commissioner . The High Court dismissed the appeal . It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the deity did not have any right to be registered as a public Trust under the Act ; that the institution of the suit was a private trust and it was not necessary for the trustee to establish the same ; that there was no evidence of any nuisance or danger to the deity ; that even if the ded ication is proved to be a public endowment , the fact that the ded ic ant was a public temple could not be established ; that since the ded anc ers were not the owner of the property , they were not entitled to claim any share in the property ; that in the absence of any evidence regarding the existence of the ded ance , the question of title does not arise ; that as the ded icate es were not owners of the properties , the mere fact that they were attached to the property would not make them liable to be prosecuted under the provisions thereof . Held : ( i ) that the expression ' public trust ' in section 5 of the , means a trust which is intended to be used for the purpose of promoting the objects of the trust ; and ( ii ) that in order to enable the trustee of the endowment to administer the trust property , the trust must be shown to exist and the trustees are required to act fairly . The word " public trust " in section 7 of the means a public char ity and includes a public math . The words " public char ities " do not mean a public chari ties

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 1952 1952 by the Third Income tax Officer , C 1 Ward , Bombay . In respect of his own business he was assessed as a result of which he had been sentenced to pay a fine of Rs . 40 , 178 4 . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Superintendent of Estate , but in appeal the Collector held that the assessee was not liable to be prosecuted under section 13 ( 2 ) of the Act because it was not proved that the income from the business was exempt from liability to tax . On appeal the Appellate Tribunal upheld the view taken by the authorities below . It also held that there was no evidence on record to show that the appellant was guilty of concealment or suppression of facts . Held , that the expression " concealment " used in section 13 of the Indian Income Tax Act is wide enough to include any omission or commission on the part of the assessee . The word " concealment ' has not been defined in the Act . The words " concealment ", " wilful default " and " willful default " are sy non y mous with " intentional default ". The term " concealment of facts " means intention to evade payment of tax . The fact that the person who made the statement was not examined before the assessing officer and the appellate authority did not examine him would not make the statement of the person making the statement inadmissible . The mere fact that he made the statements were not sufficient to cover the certified demand , does not mean that the burden of proof was on the assessee to prove that the statement had been made voluntarily . The failure to produce the books of account and other documents before the Assessing Officer could not lead to the conclusion that the maker of the statement knew what might have happened to the assessee and that the onus was discharged .

The appellants were the workmen of the Bombay Port Trust . They were employed in the Port of Bombay . The respondents to this appeal were the trustees of the Port Trust , who were employees of the appellant company . The dispute was referred by the Government of India under section 10 ( 2 ) of the Industrial Disputes Act , 1947 for adjudication . The Tribunal held that the Union had not been able to establish that the existing system of work required any modification . The Appellate Tribunal found that the union had under its control several doc ks and it had under their control various doc ks . Reference in this connection was made to the Prince ' s and Vict oria Doc ks . The question was whether the new system of working of the shore crew at all these places was a part of the port of work . Held , that the decision of the Central Government Industrial Tribunal is right in law . It is open to the parties to raise disputes regarding the existence or otherwise of the particular port of operations which are covered by the charter of work undertaken by them . The mere fact that the ship has been taken over by the Port Authority does not mean that the vessel should be treated as one of the ports . The Port Trust had under the control of the Government and the Port Authorities had no power to make such an order . The Sea Port Management Rules , 1960 , framed under the , were applicable to the case of the Mill .

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that he was in arrears of rent and had been paying monthly rent to the respondent . The suit was decreed by the trial court and the High Court set aside the decree and remanded the case back to the Trial Judge for fresh decision . In appeal , the High court set aside this finding of the trial judge but allowed the plaintiff ' s appeal . It held that since the premises were let out in June 1976 but as the assessment was made on October 1 , 1976 the provisions of U . P . Urban Buildings ( Regulation of Let ting , Rent and Eviction ) Act , 1972 will not apply and therefore a decree for eviction could only be passed . On appeal , it was contended before us that the rights of parties would be governed on the basis of the date on which the suit was instituted and it was urged that since there was no dispute about the date when the suit is filed by the respondent the provisions contained in section 20 of the Act would not apply . Dismis sing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The right of the landlord to evict a tenant has been provided under section 20 ( 2 )( 1 ) of the U . p . Urban Building ( Regulation Of Let ting Rent and Rent ) Act 1972 . [ 10 89 D ] 2 . Section 20 of U P . Act provides that where any building or part thereof is required for the purpose of carrying out any work or operation in respect of which the notice referred to in sub section ( 1 ) is given , the provisions thereof shall apply to such building or portion thereof as are specified therein . [ 11 89 E F ] 3 . The language of section 20 is clear and unambiguous . If the provisions are read together with the words used in the said section , it would be clear that the restriction is to the institution of the suit itself and not of the tenants . [ 12 89 G H ; 13 90 A ] 4 . The expression " in any other manner " means that if the provisions mentioned in the section are read harmon iously , it should be construed so as to give effect to the intention of the legislature . But the word " in every case " in its ordinary sense means that the provision of law must be interpreted according to the intent of the Legislature . [ 13 91 B C ] 5 . The definition of the term " occupation " in section 2 ( c ) of U PC Act makes it clear that even after the determination of tenancy by efflux of time the tenant can get protection from eviction

The appellant was the th ika tenant . He filed a suit for ejectment of three persons , who were described as tenants under the plaintiff and the third respondent . The suit was decreed by a Munsif of Seal dah court on March 18 , 1949 after the Calcutta Thi ka Tenancy Act , 1949 had come into force on February 28 , 1949 . The decree holder put the decree in execution and recovered possession of the land on December 18 , 1950 . The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that section 4 of the Calcutta Chi ka Tenancy ( Amendment ) Ordinance , 1952 which came into force with effect from February 28 1949 did not apply to the case because it provided that the provisions of the West Bengal Thi ka Rent Control ( Amendment Ordinance ), 1952 would be applicable to all pre Acts instituted before the date of the commencement of the Act of 1949 . On appeal by certificate the High Court held that the appellant could not claim any right over the suit property as he had failed to establish his rights as a th ika tenancy . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts should have held that section 3 of the Bengal Thi kha Tenancy ( Second Amendment ) Act , 1953 , was prospective only and as such applies to pre Act suits and appeals pending on 21st October 1952 and not to pre s . 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure . HELD : ( i ) Section 3 of Bengal Thi sa Tenancy ( Third Amendment ) Bill , 1961 , introduced certain changes in the Act and replaced certain new definitions . The words " or otherwise " used in the said section are wide enough to cover all pre - existing cases . [ 229 E ] ( ii ) The expression " or other " is defined in the Bengal Wak fs Act , 19 11 , as meaning a person who has been convicted of an offence under the Indian Penal Code , 1860 . It does not mean a person whose conviction is based upon the fact whether he has been previously convicted or acquitted or discharged or discharged . The word " or " in the context means ' a person against whom a decree is passed '. If the person against whose acquittal is sought to be made is a party to the proceeding , the expression " any other person " must necessarily include a person claiming through him as a member of the family . [ 230 A B ]

The State Government appointed a Pay Commission with wide ranging reference . The Committee recommended for the pay scale of Rs . 160 320 as against the pay scales of Rs , 120 300 to Section Officers . The State Govt . accepted the recommendations and issued a revised pay scale . The High Court held that it was not permissible to have two pay scales in the same cadre for persons having same duties and having different qualities . The Selection Committee recommended the pay of Bench Secretaries Grade I to be placed at par with Section Officers and Private Secretaries . The recommendation made by the Pay Commission was approved by the State Government . Thereafter , the State Govt ., accepted the recommendation . Thereupon , the High Court directed that the pay fixation should be done on the basis of the recommendations of the Pay Commissions . In appeal before this Court , it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in holding that the decision of the Commission is arbitrary and based on no evidence or material . It was further urged that the State has got power to grant higher pay scale to the Bench Secretaries who are being paid similar emoluments . Allow ing the appeal , this Court ^ HELD : 1 . The classification based on experience is a reasonable classification . It has a rational nexus with the object thereof . To hold otherwise would be violative of the right to have equal pay for equal work . [ 122 F ] 2 . The principle of equal pay will apply to all other similarly situated persons . The concept of equal work is a relevant factor in determining whether a particular person is fit for such pay scale or not . If it has a scientific nexus with a purpose it requires a more skilled qualification than one , it cannot be said to be discriminatory . [ 123 E ] 3 . The doctrine of equal salary for equal pay does not apply to cases where there is a rational relation between the object of differenti ation . To do so would be creating a legitimate differentia which distinguish es persons from those who are charged with the administration in fixing their pay scales . [ 124 G H ; 125 A B ] 4 . The distinction sought to be drawn between the two classes of employees is that they are entitled to equal pay . [ 126 C D ] 5 . The difference between the nature of work and the nature and culture of employment depends upon the nature , character and pattern of work . They are the same . There is an element of value judgment of the administrative authorities who are responsible for the same and the degree of responsibility is a necessary con com it ant of the duty of the judicial authority . The appellant company was a Government Company incorporated under the , and was vested in a Government undertaking . Respondent 1 was the State of Madhya Pradesh . On March 31 , 1976 , respondent 2 entered into an agreement with the appellant Companies for the purpose of development and use of land . Respondent 3 was the Chairman and respondent 4 was the Director of the appellant Company . Respondent 5 was the Secretary of the Board of Directors of the Company . The appellant Company was a government company incorporated under section 65 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar T atha Gram Niv esh Adhiniyam , 1973 . It was registered as a company under the provisions of the U . P . Sugar Undertakings ( Acquisition ) Ordinance , 1971 . The Act came into force on April 30 , 1975 . The notification issued by the Central Government for acquisition of right to salt pe ter was published in the Gazette on August 8 , 1974 . The declaration made by the Parliament in respect of the said land was published on September 9 , 1974 , that it would be deemed to have been validly acquired by the State Government under the Act . The State Legislature passed the Rajasthan Land Revenue Code , 1959 , which provided for the acquisition of rights of the land held by the Government of India . Section 64 empowered the State Governments to acquire certain lands from the owner or occupier thereof .
